caption:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the Nvidia scandal is not really about Jensen Huang's affair.
On CNBC he asked whether Nvidia knew who it was selling chips to, and blamed the Commerce Department for not blacklisting Megaspeed, a Singapore firm suspected of routing chips to China.
The Senate Banking Committee has asked Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify in December.

Who should answer for chips that end up in China: the seller or the government?

paragraphs.text: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on November 13, 2026 that the Commerce Department was responsible for not adding Megaspeed, a Singapore company linked to the Nvidia scandal, to the US trade blacklist. He made the comments on CNBC, according to AFP and International Business Times.

Bessent said the Treasury, the Defense Department, the State Department and the Office of the US Trade Representative had supported putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months. Asked why that had not happened, he said Commerce has the pen and that questions about its internal processes should go to Commerce. AFP described the remarks as a rare public rebuke of one cabinet department by another.

US authorities suspect Megaspeed of helping Chinese firms get around US export controls by buying Nvidia chips for data centers in Southeast Asia and routing them to China, AFP reported. The agency said the company traded more than $4 billion in Nvidia chips over two years. 24/7 Wall St. noted that Reuters, as cited by Newsweek, put the figure at more than $4.8 billion since June 2024.

Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing and says it cooperated with US inspections, according to International Business Times. 24/7 Wall St. reported that the company says it takes its export control obligations seriously and has hired a US law firm to review its compliance. The entity list is kept by the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, and exports to companies on it require a license.

A former Megaspeed director, Alice Huang, was identified in US media as an alleged Chinese intelligence asset who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, AFP reported. The two are not related. Beijing has denied the spying allegations. Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair in a November 8 letter to Nvidia employees and resigned as chief executive on November 12.

Bessent said coverage of the scandal had focused too much on Huang's personal life. In his view, the questions that matter are whether Nvidia knew its client and whether it made a serious effort to prevent chips from leaking to China. He questioned whether Nvidia had sold to pass-through shell companies and said anyone at the company responsible should be held accountable, according to AFP and International Business Times.

Bessent also said he was frustrated because President Donald Trump had made clear that China should not receive Nvidia chips more advanced than the H100. He said there is a lot of leakage in the system and that the administration is working to close it. 24/7 Wall St. reported that he expects Nvidia's board to conduct a thorough investigation.

Axios had reported that Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in a White House Situation Room meeting the week before, International Business Times said. A Commerce spokeswoman, Kristen Eichamer, denied that the exchange took place. Bessent declined to describe the meeting, and a White House official said Trump has complete confidence in Lutnick, according to 24/7 Wall St.

The Senate Banking Committee has asked Huang and Lutnick to testify, according to International Business Times and 24/7 Wall St., which reported the dates as December 3 for Huang and December 10 for Lutnick. Commerce said Lutnick agreed to appear voluntarily. The committee said it would use all tools available, including subpoenas, if needed.

The remarks shift part of the focus of the Nvidia affair away from Huang's personal conduct and toward two institutions: Nvidia's own customer checks and the Commerce Department's export enforcement. Each side now has reason to point at the other in the coming hearings.
Watch for a Federal Register notice adding Megaspeed to the entity list, the findings of Nvidia's board review, and the Senate Banking hearings with Huang and Lutnick in December.
